Each cat is represented by a unique tile and belongs to a family; you must find a way to make them all fit on your boat while keeping families together. The Isle of Cats Duel replaces the card drafting from the original The Isle of Cats game with a new movement system. Guided by an Oshax cat, players take turns moving around the island. Where you move determines which cats, treasures, and lessons you can access and will shape the options available to your opponent on their next turn. In the end, the player who best balances rescuing cats, completing lessons, and limiting their opponent's options will prove themselves as the ultimate cat rescuer. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Game Overview 2 Goal of the Game 3 Gameplay 3.1 A Player's Turn 3.2 Fish Actions 3.3 Board Placement Rules 4 Special Rules 5 End of Game & Scoring 6 Tie-breaker Game Overview Hoping to rescue the legendary cats of the island before the arrival of the sinister Vesh, you navigate your boats to the shore. You must bring as many cats as possible on board, group them into families, and learn valuable lessons to optimize your boat's layout. This is achieved through clever resource management and tile-placement puzzles on your personal boat board. Goal of the Game Collect the most points by rescuing cat families, completing lessons, and gathering treasures, while avoiding penalties for rats and empty rooms. Gameplay The game is played over 4 rounds. During your turn, you use your resources to load the boat: A Player's Turn move the Oshax two spaces collect one of the spaces. Rescue Cats: Select cat from the board. A cat with a fish will give you one fish when you place the tile. Lessons: B lue lesson cards grants specific bonus points at the end of the game for certain formations or collections. Treasures: Treasures are yellow cards that help you fill small gaps or cover rats. Fish Actions Fish are a resource used to perform additional actions during a turn. Fish gained during a turn can be spent immediately, and unused fish are carried over to the following rounds. Spend 1 fish: Move the Oshax 1 extra space . Spend 2 fish: Jump the Oshax to any space on the island. The spaces jumped over are not considered touched. Spend 2 fish: Take 1 treasure directly from the supply and place it on your boat. Spend 3 fish: Take 1 additional discovery (cat, treasure, lesson, or instant card) in addition to your normal selection. Board Placement Rules The first tile may be placed anywhere on the boat. Every subsequent tile must be placed directly adjacent to an already placed tile (sharing a side; diagonal does not count). Cat Families: Connect cats of the same color. A group of at least 3 directly adjacent cats forms a valuable family. Special Rules The Oshax: These rare white cats are highly adaptable. When they board your boat, you choose a color for them, which they permanently keep as a wild for that family. Rat Infestation: Every visible rat on your deck disturbs the cats and results in a 1 point penalty at the end. Filling Rooms: The boat is divided into sections called rooms. Only a room completely covered by tiles avoids the penalty for "incomplete areas." End of Game & Scoring The game ends when the island is empty or no more moves are possible. Category Points Cat Families Points based on the number of cats per color (starting at 3 cats). Completed Lessons Points according to the conditions on your cards. Rats & Empty Rooms -1 per rat; -5 per incomplete room. Tie-breaker In the event of a tie, the player with the most remaining fish in their supply wins. [Rating: 4/10] Not a fan of this game. Boring theme in my opinion.  There are much better tile laying games out there. Dont waste your time

[Rating: 5/10] This was such a stress-inducing experience for what is supposed to be a calming game. In each round, you draft either a cat or a scoring card. The cats are polyomino-shaped, and you must fit them on your ship as neatly as possible to minimize negative points. However, this is no easy task, as the cats have very irregular shapes and must be placed next to one another (not just anywhere you like). Finding the least damaging spot for a cat each round was torture for an order-obsessed person like me. Scoring cards are the key to victory. [Rating: 5/10] A fun and accessible version of Isle of Cats. But... the bigger game's been out for a while and in my experience is often available at the same price or even cheaper. So no real reason to buy this unless it's to gift as a more accessible version to someone.

[Rating: 5/10] I love polyomino games. And I like the puzzles in this one too.   But the scoring cards come out during play. Which means that they can be good or bad for you. And if they are too good for your opponent, you must take them away. Even if it doesn't benefit you at all.   I never like that in games. So for me it takes away a big part of the fun.

[Rating: 5/10] I find the movement of the Oshax cat  very frustrating and not fun at all Also, this game is quite ugly looking  Definitely not for me

[Rating: 5/10] It's fine for a simplified two player version of the base game so players don't have to worry about the fish economy...but I also find it much less interesting:) Cat families felt much stronger than lessons in this version (at least in my play).

[Rating: 5/10] Not a big fan of the original but this is one of the closest to the original of a duel game I have played. Works well and is enjoyable.

[Rating: 5.2/10] I struggle to recommend [i]The Isle of Cats Duel[/i]. It's a fine game, but it doesn't offer enough distinctness to justify buying this one over other polyomino options. For a meatier puzzle, [i]Planet Unknown[/i] offers a lot more and plays well at 2 players (actually, it scales well from 1 to 6). For an entry-level 2-player-only polyomino puzzle, [i]Patchwork[/i] is still the king.  Read my full review: https://shelfgamer.com/reviews/the-isle-of-cats-duel/
